source_text: Πρόσχες δὲ καὶ τῷ ἐπιπολαίῳ τοῦ περὶ τῶν τότε μαθητῶν Ἰησοῦ λόγου, ἐν ᾧ φησιν· εἶτα οἱ μὲν τότε ζῶντι αὐτῷ συνόντες καὶ τῆς φωνῆς ἐπακούοντες αὐτοῦ καὶ διδασκάλῳ χρώμενοι κολαζόμενον καὶ ἀποθνῄσκοντα ὁρῶντες οὔτε συναπέθανον οὔτε ὑπεραπέθανον αὐτοῦ οὐδὲ κολάσεων καταφρονεῖν ἐπείσθησαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἠρνήσαντο εἶναι μαθηταί· νῦν δὲ ὑμεῖς αὐτῷ συναποθνῄσκετε. καὶ ἐν τούτοις δὲ τὸ μὲν ἔτι εἰσαγομένοις τοῖς μαθηταῖς καὶ ἀτελεστέροις οὖσιν ἁμαρτηθὲν καὶ γεγραμμένον ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις πιστεύει γεγονέναι, ἵν᾿ ἐγκαλῇ τῷ λόγῳ, τὸ δὲ μετὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν αὐτοῖς κατορθωθὲν παῤῥησιασαμένοις ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίων καὶ μυρία ὅσα πεπονθόσιν ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνων καὶ τὸ τελευταῖον ἀποθανοῦσιν ὑπὲρ τῆς Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίας παρασιωπᾷ. οὔτε γὰρ Ἰησοῦ ἐβουλήθη ἀκοῦσαι προλέγοντος τῷ Πέτρῳ· „ὅταν δὲ γηράσῃς, ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς σου“ καὶ τὸ ἑξῆς, ᾧ ἐπιφέρει ἡ γραφή· „τοῦτο δ᾿ εἶπε σημαίνων, ποίῳ θανάτῳ δοξάσει τὸν θεόν“ οὔθ᾿ ὅτι Ἰάκωβος ὁ ἀδελφὸς Ἰωάννου, ἀπόστολος ἀποστόλου ἀδελφὸς, ἀνῃρέθη ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἡρώδου διὰ τὸν λόγον Χριστοῦ „μαχαίρᾳ“· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ὅσα παῤῥησιαζόμενοι ἐπὶ τῷ λόγῳ πεποιήκασιν ὁ Πέτρος καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ ἀπόστολοι, καὶ ὡς „ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ συνεδρίου“ ἐξῆλθον μετὰ τὸ μαστιγωθῆναι „χαίροντες,“ „ὅτι κατηξιώθησαν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος ἀτιμασθῆναι,“ καὶ ὑπεραίροντες πολλὰ τῶν παρ᾿ Ἕλλησιν ἱστορουμένων ἐπὶ τῇ καρτερίᾳ καὶ ἀνδρίᾳ τῶν φιλοσοφησάντων. ἀρχῆθεν οὖν τοῦτο μάλιστα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μάθημα ἐκρατύνετο παρὰ τοῖς ἀκούουσιν αὐτοῦ, διδάσκον καταφρονεῖσθαι μὲν τὸ ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν περιεπόμενον ζῆν, σπουδάζεσθαι δὲ τὸ παραπλήσιον τῷ ζῆν τοῦ θεοῦ ζῆν.
pass_a_gloss: Attend (προσέχω) also to the superficiality (ἐπιπόλαιον) of the account (λόγος) concerning the disciples of Jesus at that time, in which he says: then those being with (σύνειμι) him then living, and hearing his voice (φωνή), and using [him as] teacher (διδάσκαλος), seeing [him] punished (κολάζω) and dying, neither died with (συναποθνῄσκω) nor died for (ὑπεραποθνῄσκω) him, nor were persuaded to despise (καταφρονέω) punishments (κολάσεις), but even denied (ἀρνέομαι) being disciples; but now you die with him. And in these the sin (ἁμαρτάνω) of the disciples, still being introduced/beginners (εἰσάγω) and being more imperfect (ἀτελής), and written in the Gospels, he believes (πιστεύω) to have happened, in order that he may accuse (ἐγκαλέω) the doctrine (λόγος); but the thing accomplished rightly (κατορθόω) by them after the sin, having spoken boldly (παρρησιάζομαι) before Jews and having suffered countless things by them and finally having died on behalf of the teaching (διδασκαλία) of Jesus, he passes over in silence (παρασιωπάω). For neither did he wish to hear Jesus foretelling (προλέγω) to Peter: "but when you grow old (γηράσκω), you will stretch out (ἐκτείνω) your hands" and what follows, to which the Scripture (γραφή) adds: "this he said signifying (σημαίνω) by what death he will glorify (δοξάζω) God"; nor that James the brother of John, apostle brother of apostle, was killed (ἀναιρέω) by Herod through the word of Christ "by sword (μάχαιρα)"; but neither as many things as speaking boldly for the word Peter and the other apostles have done, and how "from the face of the council (συνέδριον)" they went out after being flogged (μαστιγόω) "rejoicing", "that they were deemed worthy (καταξιόω) to be dishonoured (ἀτιμάζω) for the name (ὄνομα)", and surpassing (ὑπεραίρω) many of the things narrated (ἱστορέω) among Greeks of the endurance (καρτερία) and courage (ἀνδρεία) of those who philosophized. From the beginning therefore this lesson (μάθημα) of Jesus most of all was strengthened (κρατύνω) among his hearers, teaching the living cherished (περιέπω) by the many to be despised (καταφρονέω), and the living near-like (παραπλήσιος) to the living of God to be striven for (σπουδάζω).
pass_b_english: Notice too how shallow his account is of the disciples Jesus had at that time, where he says: “Then those who were with him while he lived, who heard his voice and had him as their teacher, when they saw him punished and dying, neither died with him nor died for him, nor were they persuaded to despise punishments; instead they even denied that they were his disciples. But now you die with him” (compare Matthew 26:69–75). In these words he believes that the sin the disciples committed while they were still beginners and imperfect, which is written in the Gospels, did happen, so that he may accuse the teaching; but what they did rightly after the sin, when they spoke boldly before the Jews, suffered countless things at their hands and at last died for the teaching of Jesus, he passes over in silence.

For he did not wish to hear Jesus foretelling to Peter, “But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands,” and the rest (John 21:18), to which Scripture adds, “This he said to show by what death he would glorify God” (John 21:19). Nor did he wish to hear that James the brother of John, an apostle and the brother of an apostle, was put to death by Herod “with the sword” for the word of Christ (Acts 12:2). Nor did he wish to hear all that Peter and the other apostles did as they spoke boldly for the word, and how, after being flogged, they went out “from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name” (Acts 5:40–41), surpassing many of the stories told among the Greeks of the endurance and courage of those who practised philosophy.

From the beginning, then, this lesson of Jesus above all took firm hold among those who heard him: it taught them to despise the life that the many cling to, and to strive for a life that is like the life of God.

choices.why: "less perfect" made "imperfect"; μέν/δέ contrast kept in one sentence
"what they achieved after the sin" made "what they did rightly after the sin" (κατορθωθέν)
John 21:18, 21:19, Acts 12:2, Acts 5:40-41 and the Matthew 26:69-75 allusion checked against the verses

translator_notes: Celsus’s words (from εἶτα to συναποθνῄσκετε) are quoted directly. His “they denied that they were disciples” alludes to Peter’s denial (Matthew 26:69–75 and parallels); the citation is placed after the quotation to keep Celsus’s words intact. John 21:18–19 and Acts 5:41 are quoted closely; ἀτιμασθῆναι is rendered “to suffer dishonour”; the flogging is Acts 5:40. James’s death “with the sword” is Acts 12:2. εἰσαγομένοις (“being introduced”, i.e. still under instruction) is rendered “beginners”, and ἀτελεστέροις “imperfect”. The two halves of the sentence (τὸ μὲν ... πιστεύει γεγονέναι ... τὸ δὲ ... παρασιωπᾷ) are kept in one sentence to keep Origen’s contrast. τὸ παραπλήσιον τῷ ζῆν τοῦ θεοῦ ζῆν is rendered “a life that is like the life of God”.
